findings.reason: the plan claims each clause has its own negative control, and without a named probe path the two controls cross-fire, so the recorded evidence would not say which clause the failure belonged to.
findings.text: the changed port clause records and gates "how long the port takes … to answer its first request with 200" without naming the request, while its sibling clause's probe path is `/_index` and §2's landed gate for the same property asks `/_projects/mounts.json`. A reporter who takes the port's first request to be an `/_index` read couples the port gate to the `/_index` clause: in the `/_index` control arm (index removed, no mutation) that read pays the same cold rebuild, so the port gate can fail there too, and a failure under one control stops identifying the clause it belongs to. Naming the probe (§2's `/_projects/mounts.json`, or any non-index route) restores two independently falsifiable clauses.

findings.reason: §7 already cites "§2's control mutation", and §2's landed record pins that mutation precisely (arm every tree on the calling thread after the bind, before `serve_forever`), so the worker builds the control that makes the gate fail either way; only the summary wording is off.
findings.text: the newly added justification for the measure ("the socket listens before the server serves") and the port control's stated mutation ("`_FleetChangeWatch.start` arms the watch before the port binds") describe two different start modes: the first holds only when the socket is already bound (as the landed `main` has it — bind at `reckon/serve.py:4134`, watch at `4137`, `serve_forever` at `4151`), the second is a mode the tree cannot produce. A worker following the words moves `start_fleet_change_watch` above the `ThreadingHTTPServer` construction, where the socket never listens.
